studies.title: Stand, Except A Little
studies.meaning: The address names a posture rather than a rank, and the commentators read it as a description of what the man was actually doing when this came. What follows is an instruction with latitude built into it: stand at night, about half, or somewhat less, or somewhat more. The measure is deliberately loose. A manner is then specified, the recitation given evenly and unhurried. The reason arrives last and reframes everything before it: something heavy is coming, and this is the preparation for carrying it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, among the earliest surahs and close to the start of the mission. The sources describe the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) wrapping himself up after an early encounter with revelation, and they read the opening address against that scene. What is asked here is a long night of standing. The surah's closing ayah, which the classical accounts place about a year later, lifts the requirement, so the chapter keeps both the demand and its relief.

keyTerms.note: A participle for a man who has wrapped himself into his clothes. The form implies doing it to yourself, which is why the commentators take the address as a picture of a posture rather than a title of office.
The root evokes teeth set evenly spaced in a jaw. It asks for even, unhurried delivery with every part distinct, and Arabic later took the name of the whole discipline of recitation from this word.
A plain word for physical weight, used of loads a camel carries. Applied to speech it keeps the metaphor bodily: what is coming has to be borne, not merely understood or agreed with.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Nights in the Meccan valley were long and cold, and a man slept in the cloak he had worn all day, drawing it over his head against the chill. Wrapping up was what you did to sleep. It was also what you did when you were frightened or ill and wanted the room shut out, and everybody understood the gesture without asking. The instruction arrives at exactly that moment and asks the man to come out from under it and stand.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for measured recitation occurs twice in the Quran. Once here, as an instruction to the man receiving the revelation. Once in another surah, where God says of the revelation itself that He sent it down in exactly that manner. The same term describes the sending and the receiving, from the two ends of the same act.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The order of the sentences is the argument. The practice is commanded first and the reason supplied last, so the reader watches a preparation being set up before learning what it prepares for. Revelation is then described as a weight rather than as a comfort or a distinction, which makes prophecy a burden with a training regime attached to it. And the latitude in the measure puts flexibility into the demand from the very beginning.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for measured delivery, there of how the revelation was sent down.
Gives the weight of the revelation an image: a mountain would split apart under it.
Describes the recitation as given in portions so that it could be delivered slowly.

studies.applyIt: Read one page of the Quran tonight at half your usual speed. Not with more feeling, simply slower, with the pauses taken where they fall. This passage is about pace before it is about anything else. Notice which words you have been sliding past for years, not because they are difficult, but because you never gave them the time to arrive.

studies.title: The Hours That Weigh More
studies.meaning: A reason is given for a night practice, not an order repeated. The hours after sleep are called heavier in their tread and straighter in speech. Those are two claims about what a body and a tongue do at that hour. The day is acknowledged, not dismissed. There is a long swim of business in it. What is asked for is a devotion named with a word for cutting yourself away. The passage ends by naming God as the one to be appointed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and among the earliest surahs. At this stage the night vigil described here was a practice the small community kept for a long stretch of the night. The surah's last ayah later eases it. The passage belongs to the time when the community was small enough to gather at night unnoticed, and when the daytime was spent under pressure.

keyTerms.note: A participle for something that comes up or begins. Early scholars take it as the hours of night that arrive after sleep, or as the person who rises in them, and both readings are recorded.
The first word is used of swimming and of a horse ranging freely. Applied to the day it pictures activity that carries a person along, which is exactly why the night is offered instead.
From a root meaning to cut something off cleanly, used of separating a branch from a tree. The Arabic repeats the word in a second form for emphasis, so the cutting is stated twice.
The word for someone appointed to handle your affairs and act in your name. Taking God as that is a transfer of management, which is a different image from taking Him as a helper.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca at night was quiet in a way that is hard to reproduce now. No artificial light, no traffic, and a town small enough that a raised voice carried across it. Reciting aloud in the dark was audible to neighbours, which is part of why the practice mattered and part of why it was risky. The daytime, by contrast, was market, argument and pressure without pause.
studies.didYouKnow: The opening of this surah sets a night practice. Its last ayah lifts the requirement. Early sources report that about a year separated the two. So the surah as it stands holds both the demand and its relief in one chapter. That is unusual. A reader gets the order and the easing in a single reading.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage argues from effect rather than from authority. It does not say the night is holier; it says that at that hour the correspondence between what a person intends and what they manage is closer. That is a claim about human beings, and it is checkable. The day is then given its due in the same breath, so the vigil is positioned as preparation for work rather than as an escape from it.

crossReferences.why: Closes the same chapter by lifting the measure, naming illness, travel and fighting as reasons.
Gives the same practice as an addition rather than a requirement, with a promised standing attached.
Describes the same hours as a habit of the righteous rather than as an instruction to one person.

studies.applyIt: Say one thing out loud tonight that you would normally only think, a request, a sentence of the Quran, a plain admission. The ayah claims that words are straighter at that hour, and the only way to find out is to produce some. Ten seconds is enough, and the room being dark is part of the arrangement.
studies.explainEasier: God tells his messenger that the night is the best time to pray and to read. The day is full of work. He says to keep God's name in mind, to give himself fully to God, and to trust him.

studies.title: Withdraw Without A Word
studies.meaning: Two instructions, and the second is the stranger one. Endure what is said, then withdraw in a manner the Arabic calls beautiful: a parting with no rebuke in it and no scene made. After that the matter is taken out of his hands entirely and left to God. Commentators note that what follows is addressed to the man told to be patient rather than to his opponents, so the consequences listed work as reassurance rather than as threat. The opponents are named by their comfort, not by their belief.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early, when the community had no power to answer anything said against it and very little protection. The mockery recorded across the surrounding surahs came largely from men of standing and wealth in the town, which is how this passage identifies them. The instruction to withdraw belongs to that period specifically. No occasion is reported for these particular ayat beyond the general pressure of the Meccan years.

keyTerms.note: The noun is the word for departure and separation; the adjective is the ordinary word for beauty. Together they ask for a parting with nothing added to it, which is a demand about manner rather than about distance.

The phrase names the opponents by their comfort rather than by their position. The noun covers soft living and plenty, so the obstacle is located in what they have rather than in what they have concluded.
From a root for restraint, which also gives the word for the bit placed in a horse's mouth. It names irons that stop movement, and it occurs once in the whole Quran.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A public quarrel in Mecca was a matter of record. Insults were composed in verse, memorised, and repeated at market and at the seasonal fairs, and a man's standing depended on answering them in kind. Silence was read as defeat, not as dignity. What this passage asks for, absorbing the insult, leaving without a reply, and not making the leaving a statement either, cut directly against the strongest reflex of the culture it was spoken into.
studies.didYouKnow: The adjective for beautiful attaches to this kind of doubled construction four times in the Quran, and every time it qualifies an act of letting go: a patient endurance, a withdrawal from opponents, and twice a release at the end of a marriage. The word never describes a thing in these places. It describes the manner of a parting.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Responsibility shifts in the middle of the passage. Leaving the matter to God removes both the duty and the right to answer, which makes patience a transfer rather than a suppression. The consequences listed immediately afterwards are spoken to the injured party, so the passage treats knowing that justice exists as the thing that makes restraint bearable. It never asks him to stop minding what was said.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction in three words: be patient with a beautiful patience.
Tells him to proclaim openly and promises that God suffices against those who mock.
Shows the servants of the Merciful answering the ignorant with a word of peace.

studies.applyIt: Think of the last thing said about you that you are still drafting a reply to. You have probably written it three times in your head today. Let one round go by without answering, and notice that the silence is not the same thing as agreeing. The passage asks for a parting with no rebuke in it, which is harder than either fighting back or sulking.

studies.title: As We Sent To Pharaoh
studies.meaning: A comparison is drawn with a very particular shape. The audience is told a messenger has been sent to them, and the parallel offered is not a doubting people but the figure in the Quran's memory with the most power and the least excuse. The messenger is called a witness over them, which makes his presence evidentiary rather than only instructive. The closing sentence supplies the outcome in three Arabic words, using a construction that repeats the verb as its own object and adds no detail at all.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early. The opposition in Mecca included men whose wealth and position made a comparison with a king pointed, and the preceding ayat have just named them by their ease. The Pharaoh narrative was known in outline across the peninsula through the Jewish and Christian communities settled there, so the reference works as shorthand. Nothing more specific is reported as an occasion for these three ayat.

keyTerms.note: A dune of loose sand with a participle meaning made to pour. The picture is a mountain that has lost its cohesion and runs when touched, not one that has been broken. The phrase occurs once in the Quran.
The legal word for one who testifies from having been present. It makes the messenger's role partly evidentiary: he is among them so that what happened can be attested to afterwards.
Its root also yields the word for a downpour heavy enough to do damage. The adjective keeps the seizure weather-like: overwhelming, arriving from above, and not open to negotiation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sand dunes were a hazard, not scenery. Caravans kept clear of the deep sand seas because a laden camel sinks in them, and men knew by the feel underfoot the difference between ground that holds and ground that gives. The image in the first of these ayat takes the most solid thing in the landscape, the rock the roads were oriented by, and gives it the behaviour of the one surface nobody could stand on.
studies.didYouKnow: The last phrase uses a construction Arabic keeps for intensity: the verb is repeated as a noun and made its own object, so the sentence says He seized him with a seizing. The Quran reaches for this pattern at moments where nothing further is going to be described. The force is carried entirely by the repetition, which is why translations have to expand it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The parallel does something specific to the audience's sense of scale. They were a town; the comparison is a kingdom. By matching their situation to Pharaoh's, the passage says the pattern does not vary with size and that power is not a factor in it. Calling the messenger a witness also changes what refusal amounts to. It is not a private judgement about a claim. It is something done in front of somebody who will be asked about it.

crossReferences.why: Tells the Pharaoh episode at length, ending in the seizure this passage summarises in a clause.
Describes each community's messenger brought forward as a witness over them on that Day.
Uses the same loss of solidity for mountains, there as tufts of carded wool.

studies.applyIt: Find the person who has been present for the last few years of your life: a spouse, a colleague, a friend you see weekly. They are a witness in the plain sense, able to testify to how you actually spend your time. Ask one of them this week what they would say. Most of us have never once checked our own account against a second reader.

studies.title: A Day That Greys The Children
studies.meaning: The question is left unanswered, which is its function. Then a single image carries the whole description: a day that turns children grey. Commentators divide over whether this is meant literally or is a known Arabic figure for a calamity severe enough to age whoever it touches, and most give both readings without settling between them. The sequence then closes by releasing all the pressure it has built. The warning is called a reminder, and the last clause hands the matter over to whoever wants the road.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early. The surah has moved from a night practice through instructions on endurance into warning, and this passage closes that sequence before the long final ayah changes the register entirely. The address is in the second person plural and is aimed at the town's leadership. No particular occasion is reported; the setting is the open Meccan argument about whether the dead are raised at all.

keyTerms.note: A plural of the word for a man whose hair has whitened. Set directly against a word for young children, it compresses an entire lifetime into a single day and needs no further explanation to work.
From a root for cleaving open, which also gives the word for the original disposition a thing is made with and the name of the breaking of the fast. What splits here splits along its own seams.
The noun names something that brings back to mind what was already known. Calling the warning this assumes the hearer is not being informed but recalled to something he has allowed to slip.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Grey hair was a public fact about a man. It marked the point where he moved out of fighting age and into the council of elders, and poets used the first white hairs as the occasion for a reckoning with a life spent. A child with white hair was not a picture anyone in that world had a category for, which is exactly why the image works. It forces two ages into one body.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for grey hair occurs twice in the Quran. Once here, of children on that Day. Once in the mouth of Zechariah, an old man praying for a son, describing his own head as having caught fire with white. The same word carries a long life arriving at its natural end and a childhood ending in an afternoon.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage removes compulsion at exactly the point where the pressure is highest. Three ayat of imagery build a case, and then the whole thing is labelled a reminder and handed over to the hearer's will. That sequence recurs across the Quran and it defines how warning is meant to function: it supplies information and leaves the decision intact. Fear is used to inform a choice, never to substitute for one.

crossReferences.why: Closes with the identical formula: this is a reminder, so whoever wills takes a path.
Opens with the sky splitting, using the same root as the second ayah here.
Describes the Hour's terror with nursing mothers who forget the infants they are feeding.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you already know you should change and have known for years. The passage calls itself a reminder rather than news, so the honest response is not to learn something but to admit you had it all along. Say the sentence to yourself plainly today: I have known this for a long time. Then take one step the size of an hour.

studies.title: Read What You Can
studies.meaning: The longest ayah in the surah is a run of concessions. Each one opens with something God knows. He knows what you have been doing. He knows you cannot keep up the count. He knows some will be ill, some travelling to trade, some fighting. The measure is swapped for what is manageable, twice. Then five short orders close the surah. The last is to seek forgiveness, which early scholars note comes after a concession, not after a fault.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan by most accounts, though some early authorities place this ayah in Medina because it mentions fighting. The reports differ. The classical sources put it about a year after the opening of the surah. It speaks to a community that had been standing much of the night and could no longer keep it up. The mention of travel for trade names the ordinary pressure on Meccan believers.

keyTerms.note: A verb of counting and reckoning. What is conceded is not weakness of will but the impossibility of measuring night hours without a clock, which is a practical difficulty rather than a moral one.
The verb of repentance, used here with God as its subject. When God is the one turning, the sense is relenting and accepting, so the word for a person's return is used for the movement the other way.

keyTerms.gloss: what is easy, what is manageable
keyTerms.note: A verb meaning for something to become easy of itself. The measure is not a quantity but a threshold of effort, and the phrase is repeated in the same ayah, which is rare.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: There was no way to know the hour at night. People judged it by the position of stars, and a person waking to pray had to guess whether a third or a half of the night had passed. Standing for a measured portion was therefore genuinely impossible to do accurately, and this ayah says so. The three groups it names, the sick, the traveller and the fighter, were the three reasons a person missed anything.
studies.didYouKnow: This part of the Quran is built from short rhymed lines. This one ayah runs on for the length of a page. The change of texture is part of the effect. The opening ayat used the surah's rhythm to carry a demand. Here the rhythm breaks down into plain long prose, at exactly the point where the demand is lifted.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Every concession here rests on knowledge rather than on leniency. The verb repeats: He knows, He knows, He knows. That makes the easing an act of accuracy about people, not a softening of a standard. Those are different things to receive. The order to seek forgiveness at the end is then striking, since nothing has been done wrong. Early scholars take it as the ordinary posture of a servant.

crossReferences.why: Sets the measure this ayah replaces, half the night or a little less or a little more.
States the principle this ayah applies to a specific practice, a demand matched to what people can hold.
Puts the same easing in general terms, denying that difficulty was placed in the path deliberately.

studies.applyIt: If you have quietly dropped a practice because you could not keep it at the level you set, restart it this week at a tenth of that size. Not as a compromise. This ayah swaps a measured portion for whatever is manageable, and calls that knowledge rather than indulgence. So the smaller version is the instruction, not the excuse.
studies.explainEasier: God knows people have been praying for much of the night, and that they cannot keep it up. So he tells them to read what they can. He tells them to pray, to give, and to ask him for pardon.
